output.title: Why proof-of-concept debt survives
output.body:
Proof-of-concept debt usually survives for one boring reason: the pilot solved a slice of the problem, but nobody made it part of daily work. A small business can run the manual version for weeks, build a clever demo, and still keep the old process because the last mile is where the real cost sits: who owns it, who watches it, and who fixes it when it breaks.

That is the bounded decision I’d look at first. Not “should we use AI everywhere?” but “does this recurring workflow have a clear owner if we automate it?” If the answer is fuzzy, the pilot tends to sit on the shelf. Shelf-ware is just debt with nicer phrasing.

For an owner-operator, the comparison is simple: keep paying in time and attention for manual work, or invest in a narrow automation that fits one repeatable workflow. Bareni’s diagnostic is designed around that question. It identifies one recurring workflow, checks honestly whether AI fits, and then defines scope, fixed price, and measures if it does. Finished code and accounts stay in the customer’s name; there is no separate formal build gate.

The practical next step is to pick one workflow you repeat every week — customer questions, invoice entry, lead routing, or data sync — and ask: once this is automated, who owns running it day to day? If you cannot name that person, the problem is not the model. It is the operating decision.
